t: Malacca's rise rested on Ming protection: Zheng He called there in 1407, and in exchange for regular tribute the Yongle Emperor shielded Parameswara from the threat of Siamese attack.

Under Mansur Shah (r. 1459–1477) Malacca conquered Pahang, received Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan from Majapahit and vassalised Siak, ruling much of the Malay Peninsula and the east coast of Sumatra.

Malacca became the centre of Islamic learning in the archipelago; Classical Malay became the lingua franca of Maritime Southeast Asia and Jawi script the medium of its religious and intellectual exchange.
dyk: Afonso de Albuquerque said that taking Malacca from the Moors would ruin Cairo and Mecca and leave Venice no spices but what her merchants bought in Portugal; Tomé Pires wrote that "whoever is lord of Malacca shall have his hands on the throat of Venice".
ev: Parameswara, fleeing the sack of Singapura, founds Malacca at a fishing village of the Orang Laut at the mouth of the Bertam River.
The Yongle Emperor sends Yin Qing to Malacca; Zheng He follows in 1407 and takes Parameswara to China, recognising him as its ruler.
Raja Tengah takes the name Muhammad Shah and the title Sultan, Islamises the administration and issues the Maritime Laws of Malacca.
Ayutthaya invades by land and is beaten with the help of Tun Perak, who becomes Bendahara; a Siamese naval attack is repelled at Batu Pahat in 1456.
Mansur Shah conquers Pahang with a fleet of 200 ships and gains Indragiri, Jambi, Tungkal and Siantan from Majapahit; he dies at the peak of Malacca's splendour.
On 1 August Diogo Lopes de Sequeira arrives from Portugal; a plot to kill him fails, but several of his men are taken captive.
On 15 August Afonso de Albuquerque captures Malacca after a failed assault on 25 July; Mahmud Shah flees south.
The Portuguese raze Mahmud Shah's base at Bintan; he dies at Kampar two years later, and his sons found the Sultanates of Perak and Johor.

f.capital: Malacca (Melaka), at the mouth of the Bertam River, the modern Malacca River
f.founder: Parameswara, the last king of Singapura, known in Malay sources as Iskandar Shah
f.predecessor: The Kingdom of Singapura, sacked in 1398; before it Srivijaya and the princes of Palembang
f.successor: Portuguese Malacca (1511–1641); the Sultanates of Johor and Perak founded by the sons of Mahmud Shah
